#2095. Pressing with intensity, getting runners beyond Kane and playing like a 'Premier League team': How Thomas Tuchel's new-look England dismantled Spain - and what he's learned from cowardly retreat against Argentina

Published: 12:59 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 12:59 EST, 16 November 2026

By the end of the World Cup, it felt as if Argentina had ripped the mask off Thomas Tuchel’s England only to reveal Gareth Southgate’s England standing there blinking right back at them.

On the biggest stage, against the biggest teams, under the biggest pressure, England wilted as they always did. They sat back, they were too cautious, and they lost. And yet, ever since, Tuchel has turned England into a free-scoring winning machine, topped off by a famous victory in Madrid, ending Spain’s 43-match unbeaten streak.

In the six games since the summer, England have scored 19 goals and conceded six. Five of those have been against the world champions.

Yes, this was the Nations League and not a World Cup semi-final. No, it wasn’t at the end of a gruelling five weeks of heat, humidity and altitude. And, yes, it was only a terrific late double save from James Trafford that stopped this being yet another tale of self-sabotaging England, thanks to Elliot Anderson’s red card, blowing another lead when under pressure.

But, this time, England did see it out. They secured Tuchel’s biggest win as England boss and, in doing so, showed us just how he’s been able to get his side playing his way.

Harry Kane leads the England celebrations after his side's victory over Spain in Madrid on Sunday night

Remember when everyone used to lose their minds whenever Harry Kane dropped deep in big games under Southgate? He’s our bloody striker, for goodness sake. Get in the box!

After England’s defeat by Spain in the Euro 2024 final two years ago, Opta posted on X that Kane had touched the ball just once in the opposition box across both that game and their previous final heartbreak against Italy three years earlier.

‘One fewer than Jack Grealish,’ the post continued. ‘Grealish played 21 minutes in the 2020 final and didn't make the Euro 2024 squad.’

Ballon d’Or winner Kane has made it quite clear since that he doesn’t need to spend all his time in the box to influence games. When he drops deeper, Kane is able to show the full extent of his creativity and range of passing.

The main problem with the ploy under Southgate, however, was that Kane rarely had the team-mates to make the right runs ahead of him. He was surrounded by players who wanted to take up similar positions. Just look at the average position maps (below) from England’s loss to Spain at Euro 2024 compared to last night.

The average position map of England’s players in the loss to Spain at Euro 2024 show how Kane dropped deep, without team-mates making runs for him to exploit

...whereas on Sunday night he had runners - Anthony Gordon, Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers - around and beyond him

Two years ago, the only player who averaged their touches ahead of Kane was Bukayo Saka. Jude Bellingham was out wide. Kobbie Mainoo and Phil Foden were basically in Kane’s shadow.

On Sunday night, he had Anthony Gordon, the brilliant, belligerent Bellingham and Morgan Rogers all ahead of him – and nearly even Ben White.

That desire, and instruction, to flock forward under Tuchel has made such a difference.

Take England’s third goal (below). Kane has the ball outside the area. Rogers is bombing on to his left. Gordon, who started as a winger but finds himself occupying the central spaces Kane leaves behind, darts into the box and points to where he wants it.

Bellingham is demanding the ball, too, showing Kane he wants it to feet. Even Anderson is charging into the box. Kane finds Bellingham, who feeds the unseen White, sprinting forward on the overlap to finish.

Kane picks up the ball and is met with an array of options in front of him, ahead of England's third goal

He did similar in the win against Croatia a few days earlier, too.

Kane collects the ball deep with four bodies ahead of him, including full backs Lewis Hall and Trent Alexander-Arnold.

It his raking pass to the back post which allows Bellingham to set up Rogers to finish.

Kane's lofted pass to Rogers (top right) leads to a goal against Croatia for Bellingham (edge of box)

England’s fluidity in the final third is bamboozling defences. That is how you get the best of Kane’s creativity.

Football is changing, so Pep Guardiola told us all in January last year. The modern game is now how teams like Bournemouth and Brighton play. The current Premier League table would suggest he had a point.

Over the past few years in the English top flight, we have seen teams move away from an obsession with keeping the ball for the sake of it and turn towards a far faster, more aggressive and more physical style of play.

Tuchel wants to take from that playbook. ‘We're at our best when we're free, physically overpowering and making it Premier League-level,’ said Kane after last month's 7-0 rout of Croatia.

In the six matches since the World Cup, Tuchel’s England are having much less of the ball than they did at the start of his reign – and now less even than under Southgate.

The key is they are becoming ever more direct with it. Tuchel wants his England to play out of the back with short passes, entice opponents on to them, but then move it through the lines at speed.

Since the World Cup, England are playing far fewer passes, but more of them into the box – to find those runners. A higher percentage of them forward. More direct attacks, moving the ball up the field at a quicker speed.

On Sunday night, they showed how Tuchel wants his side to press. ‘We were hungry in the opposition half,’ said the England boss at full time.

A fine example of that (below) came just after just six minutes. Declan Rice gives his Arsenal team-mate Martín Zubimendi no time at all on the ball inside his own area, charging him down, and forcing him to play out to another Gunner in Mikel Merino. But he, too, is being harassed by Anderson and eventually England win it back and set up Kane for a chance that he fizzes wide.

A half-fit Rice was unable to apply that pressure in the summer.

Declan Rice charges forward to close down Martin Zubimendi who has possession just inside the Spanish box with Kane and Bellingham already engaged in a high press...

...Zubimendi passes to Mikel Merino but Elliot Anderson is all over him and it leads to Kane shot that just fizzes wide

So much of this improvement under Tuchel into a side capable of blowing teams away can be put down to another abstract word he used post-match in Madrid: ‘brave’.

Tuchel talked in the last international break of ‘unlocking the next level’, and taking ‘calculated risks’ with a ‘man-to-man’ press in the opposition half.

Under Southgate, and certainly in the cowardly retreat against Argentina in the summer, England showed little bravery either with the ball or without it and frequently showed too much respect to those big nations.

Too safe with the ball, too afraid to give it away, and too fearful to try to win it back in case you leave yourself open.

That appears to be changing, too. There was a moment at the start of the second half when Bellingham tried a risky through-ball to Rogers, which failed to find its man, instead of another simple ball out wide.

It handed Spain possession cheaply. But England didn’t care because they just pounced again. Spain couldn’t deal with it. In the first half, Spain completed just 84 per cent of their passes in their own half – a place where they are usually able to knock it about at will – their lowest completion rate according to Opta since the 2010 World Cup. They didn’t have a shot on target until the penalty.

England’s defence has long been seen as the weak spot and, under Southgate, it felt as though he always would rather his attacking talents not be too frivolous for fear of exposing it.

Thomas Tuchel and Kane direct England's players to keep on the front foot during the win over Spain

Tuchel is doing the opposite. England’s expected goals soared from 1.7 per game under Southgate from the 2022 World Cup to the end of his reign, to 2.2 under Tuchel’s until this summer’s tournament. Since then, it’s jumped again to 2.8 but at the cost of what they are conceding. In his early days, England coughed up fewer good chances than under Southgate but since the World Cup has more than doubled.

He will want to get that down, of course, but when you are creating so much – and have an array of top finishers to see them off – how much will that matter to Tuchel?

Even he’s getting braver. His decision to take off Gordon for Konsa and chuck as many defenders on during England’s shrinking against Argentina looked a decision that would forever haunt Tuchel’s tenure.

Against Spain, Kane made way but Tuchel ended the game with striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin on the pitch. Against Spain, he held his nerve.

#2094. Why Emile Heskey decided Bolton Wanderers would be his final club

Former Premier League, Championship and England international forward, Emile Heskey, has revealed exactly why he opted to retire after a spell with Bolton Wanderers in the mid-2010s.

The 48-year-old turned out for some of English football's most historic clubs during a 22-year career, which included a high-profile switch from boyhood club, Leicester City, to Liverpool for £11m in the year 2000.

Heskey accumulated 62 England caps and netted seven goals during his esteemed career, as well as winning eight major honours.

Having racked up 516 appearances in the Premier League alongside 110 goals and 49 assists, Heskey then returned to Championship level for the first time in 18 years in December 2014 when he initially signed a short-term contract at the Toughsheet Community Stadium.

After leaving Liverpool in 2004, Heskey went on to feature for Birmingham City, Wigan Athletic and Aston Villa, as well as a two-season spell with Newcastle Jets of the Australian A-League between 2012 and 2014.

Returning to England in late 2014, it was confirmed the striker would sign an initial short-term contract with the Whites, who were managed by Heskey's former Leicester teammate, Neil Lennon, at the time.

During his final career stint, he was partnered with Icelandic striker, Eidur Gudjohnsen, who had returned to the North West for a second spell earlier in December 2014, with the latter providing a debut goal for Heskey against Blackburn Rovers on Boxing Day of 2014.

In total, Heskey made 48 appearances for Wanderers, but his only full season at the club and the last of his career ended in relegation to League One, before he became one of 13 players who departed upon the expiration of their contracts.

Heskey started just 15 Championship games in his final career season, scoring twice against Charlton Athletic and Brighton and Hove Albion, but had already surpassed his 38th birthday at the midpoint of the campaign.

There are several examples of one-time top-level strikers continuing to lead the line into their 40s, but speaking to current Burnley forward, Jamie Vardy, Heskey revealed how he knew it was time for him to call it quits on his playing days.

"I went to Australia for two years then came back to Bolton," he said.

"It was basically, in training, more or less, when you see young kids running past you, and you think, not 'I can't do this anymore', because I could've, and I was in good shape and I felt fine, but I didn't want people running past me and not being able to tackle and get back at them like my head was telling me I could do.

"I was like, 'Do I really want to keep going down the leagues to League One and League Two and continue there', just for what?," Heskey admitted.

Bolton fans, did Emile Heskey still impress you in his career's latter stages? Comment below!

"My boys were getting bigger, and I just decided that was enough for me. I got to 38 and probably could've played another one or two years, I think."

Vardy, 39, is known for his remarkable 200-goal exploits at Leicester, during which he won the Premier League, FA Cup, Community Shield and two Championship titles between 2012 and 2025.

However, he then admitted to Heskey that he has had similar conversations with ex-professionals who may have retired earlier in their 30s, with the Sheffield native still turning out on a regular basis in the second tier.

From Championship Golden Boot winners to cult heroes of years gone by, a number of familiar EFL names are still going strong in 2026.

There are shades between the final club stint of Heskey's career and his own, with Burnley currently in a dire predicament in the Championship after relegation from the Premier League, as they could emulate the unwanted feats of Luton Town and Leicester and become the third team to suffer successive relegations from the top-flight to League One in as many years.

Jamie Carragher believes Mauricio Pochettino has as much to prove as Manchester United, suggesting the Argentine’s reputation is not fully backed up by his achievements.

Mauricio Pochettino is preparing for his first match in charge of Manchester United against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, following his departure from the United States national team to replace Michael Carrick.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea manager has arrived at Old Trafford with plenty of experience, but Carragher believes his appointment represents an opportunity for both United and Pochettino to rebuild their reputations.

Writing in The Telegraph, the former Liverpool defender highlighted the irony of United turning to a manager whose own career needs a fresh start.

“It is ironic that in their latest attempt to rejuvenate and restore some of their old fire, Manchester United have turned to a manager whose career needs a similar reawakening,” Carragher wrote.

He suggested that Pochettino should be grateful that a club of United’s stature came calling at this stage of his career.

“Manchester United need a savior to first ease them from the relegation zone and then revive their Premier League and Champions League credibility. Pochettino, meanwhile, needed a club like United to save him from a managerial career that promised more than it delivered.”

Manchester United were fortunate to secure a manager with Pochettino’s experience after dismissing Michael Carrick so early in the season. However, he believes the Argentine has plenty to prove despite his strong reputation in the game.

“The South American returns to England with a big reputation, but not enough on his CV to back up glowing testimonials,” he continued.

Carrick believes one of the biggest concerns surrounding Pochettino is his record in important matches.

“A recurring issue with Pochettino, which continued with the US team, is an inability to get over the line in the most consequential, winnable matches, resulting in a lack of big trophies.”

Despite questioning his ability to bottle in big games, he praised his teams when everything comes in together.

“Ten years ago his best team were the embodiment of him, full of energy, style and ambition. Time will tell whether this version of Pochettino is the one turning up at Old Trafford.”

Pochettino will have the chance to shut Carragher’s doubts on Sunday when Manchester United face Liverpool. His immediate priority will be to take United out of the relegation zone, but the expectations at Old Trafford will extend far beyond survival.

The Liverpool fixture will be his first opportunity to make an impression. Carragher, however, believes the Argentine’s real challenge is to turn his reputation into success.

#2091. He scored goals for QPR and Nottingham Forest - Then tried to transform healthcare

Life after professional football has been a mixed bag for Dexter Blackstock, but the former striker has found himself a new niche in the pharmaceutical industry.

Upon first glance, the post-playing career options of the professional footballer can appear somewhat limited. Coaching or the media are the obvious options, but paid employment in these sectors can be limited, and it might not appeal to all.

But by the time that most players reach their late twenties, there may be decisions that have to be made, and in the case of Dexter Blackstock, a player who built himself a fearsome reputation as a striker with a number of clubs including Nottingham Forest and Queens Park Rangers, the decisions that he did make coupled with his entrepreneurial instincts have led him into an industry that few would have expected while he was playing.

Born in Oxford and brought up in Oxford United's youth academy, Dexter Blackstock had his first breakthrough in the senior game after transferring to Southampton in 2003. First brought into the first-team squad during an injury crisis, he came off the bench at half-time during a League Cup match in September 2004 against Colchester United with the Saints trailling by a goal to nil, scoring a second half hat-trick to help secure the Saints a 3-2 win.

Despite this - and scoring in a hotly-contested Premier League derby match with Portsmouth a couple of months later - Blackstock was unable to tie down a regular starting place in the Southampton team and, following spells on loan with Plymouth Argyle and Derby County, moved on to Queens Park Rangers in 2006.

Blackstock would go on to build his reputation further at Loftus Road, scoring 32 times in 117 appearances for QPR over the next three years. He also made two appearances for the England under-21s during this time, having also played for the under-18 and under-19 teams while at Southampton.

But in March 2009, he was sent on loan to a Nottingham Forest team that was battling to avoid relegation from the Championship, amid reports that he would be going to The City Ground permanently should they stay up. Forest ended the season in 19th place in the table, and consequently his move was made permanent that summer.

Blackstock spent seven years at Forest, with a loan spell at Leeds United in 2013. He had some problems with injuries while he was there, missing a year from November 2010 with a knee ligament injury, but still managed to score 44 goals for them in 187 appearances. And while he never got to play a full international match for England, he did also qualify to play for Antigua & Barbuda and made 12 appearances for them between 2012 and 2016.

He left Nottingham Forest by mutual consent at the end of the summer 2016 transfer window and moved on to Rotherham United, but his spell with the Millers only lasted a year before his three-year contract was mutually cancelled after a year, and he retired from the game at 31 years of age.

By the time that his playing career came to an end, Blackstock already had an idea of what he wanted to do afterwards. He'd built up a portfolio of buy-to-let properties, but his early experience as a landlord wasn't successful.

In October 2019, he was fined £24,000 at Nottingham Magistrates Court after inspectors found a number of his properties to be in a state of disrepair. He admitted 12 counts of failing to license the properties and was fined £24,000 and ordered to pay £1,100 costs and a £170 victim surcharge on top of his fine. In 2021, he was ordered to repay £8,500 in housing benefit that he'd received for the unlicensed properties.

But Blackstock's entrpreneurial leanings had by this time already taken him in a new direction. He formed MediConnect with a view towards using blockchain technology to counter the negative image that online pharmacies had received over concerns regarding a lack of controls to prevent the over-prescription of strong painkillers to customers.

At the start of 2019, Blackstock spoke to The Sun about his new business venture, and also shone a little light on the end of his playing career. “I had lost my mojo and I had no intention of carrying on playing football", he told them, "I wasn’t enjoying playing at Rotherham." On his move into pharmaceuticals, he added, "As it stands, there is nothing to stop anyone ordering drugs from one online pharmacy, then exactly the same with another company and then going down to their local GP and topping up with the same."

In 2021, Blackstock spoke to World Pharmaceutical Frontiers in greater detail about his vision. "Anyone who’s using an online pharmacy platform will need a unique customer number and every transaction will be put on the blockchain," he told them, "so the next pharmacy can check whether the patient can have that drug in the same timeframe or mix the drugs."

The previous year, at the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, he told the BBC that he was using his company to help the public donate personal protective equipment (PPE) to frontline staff dealing with the pandemic. By 2023, he had a reported net worth of £7.8 million, with The Sun reporting that, "the bulk of his earnings" was still coming "from the 50 properties he owns." If nothing else, the experience of Dexter Blackstock demonstrates that the post-career options for the professional footballer are as broad as their imaginations will let them believe.

#2088. He was a Coventry City and Aston Villa goal machine - Then invented something unusual

Dion Dublin is one of English football's most well-respected former professionals, with the 57-year-old's playing and post-playing career certainly generating plenty of interest.

The Leicester native plied his trade for some of the country's most historic clubs at various levels, including a spell in the Championship with Norwich City towards the very end of his career.

Such is his current presence, it is fair to say that those of various generations will know Dublin either for his goalscoring exploits in the 1990s and 2000s, or either as a television personality, having followed in the footsteps of various other high-profile names within the game,

However, it is fair to say that not everyone will be familiar with the former striker's attempts to forge a career in the music industry, which made headlines just over a decade ago.

From Championship Golden Boot winners to cult heroes of years gone by, a number of familiar EFL names are still going strong in 2026.

Dublin was well-travelled throughout his career, with a breakthrough spell at Cambridge United eventually paving the way for his success as a Premier League-level striker.

The Yellows climbed two divisions during the forward's time at the club between 1990 and 1992, during which he netted the first play-off final-winning strike at Wembley against Chesterfield, before being sold to Manchester United for £1m.

Dublin's Old Trafford spell has been well-documented due to a serious leg injury which pushed him below the likes of Eric Cantona in Sir Alex Ferguson's pecking order, and after two years, the striker joined Coventry City for £2m.

His goalscoring touch was then reignited at Highfield Road, netting 72 times in 162 appearances, including an 18-goal campaign in 1997/98 in which he ended as the Premier League's joint-highest scorer alongside Chris Sutton and Michael Owen.

Dublin then spent just under six years at Aston Villa under John Gregory, Graham Taylor and David O'Leary, scoring 59 times in 192 games, as well as infamously being sent off in a Second City derby defeat to Birmingham City in 2003 for headbutting Robbie Savage.

During the latter stages of his Villa spell, Dublin went on to feature in what is now the Championship on loan with Millwall in 2001/02, as the Lions made the play-offs but were defeated in agonising fashion by Birmingham at the semi-final stage.

After leaving B6 in 2004, the experienced figure moved to his hometown club, Leicester City, for two seasons, scoring six times in 42 appearances in the 2004/05 season, before featuring just 21 times the following season.

A spell with Celtic sandwiched his time at the King Power Stadium and a return to academy side, Norwich City, for two seasons where Dublin wound down his playing days between 2006 and 2008, scoring 16 times in 79 appearances, despite occasionally being drafted in to feature as a centre-back.

Dublin then became a regular fixture on television screens post-retirement, but as well as this, rediscovered his love for music, which led to an intriguing creation.

In 2013, it was revealed that the former striker had invented the 'dube' - described as a "cube-based drum played with the hands."

This led to concerts with the People's Orchestra, which revealed just how much this side of his life helped Dublin through the aforementioned difficult six-month injury setback with the Red Devils.

Did you know about Dion Dublin's musical invention? Comment below!

"Not having had the opportunity to play with a full orchestra before I am excited to be taking the Dube, the percussion drum I invented seven years ago, with me to perform on the day," he said.

Whilst Dublin's music invention is certainly lesser-known, what isn't is that the four-time England international has been a regular daytime television presenter on BBC One's 'Homes Under the Hammer'.

It was, rather unsurprisingly, baffling to many of the show's audience when the decision was made in 2015 for Dublin to join Martin Roberts and Lucy Alexander on the show, as well as his punditry roles on BBC Sport.

During his 11 years on the show, Dublin has become infamous for his line of "stairs leading up to the bedroom," but revealed that this sector is another of his great passions.

"I have a passion for property and look forward to meeting people on the show who share that passion," he said when landing this particular long-standing gig.

The former defender also highlighted Bruno Fernandes’ drop in form, suggesting the captain could benefit from a change in management.

“You have to see Bruno’s form has dropped, so it will be great to see this pick up under the new manager.”

Pochettino’s priority will be getting a response on Sunday against Liverpool from his senior players. United have been in this cycle of repeating managers and not finding much success. Mauricio Pochettino needs to take things one at a time. Sunday would be that first step.

#2086. Manchester United managerial costs near £100m as Pochettino fee revealed

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

Manchester United have spent approximately £95m appointing and dismissing managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013, according to BBC Sport, with the total expected to pass £100m following Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival.

United’s latest financial disclosures confirm a fee of £7.584m in connection with appointing Pochettino, who left his role as United States national team head coach earlier this month.

The figure takes the cumulative cost of managerial changes to around £95m, according to BBC Sport’s analysis. That total is expected to rise once the costs of Michael Carrick’s dismissal and appointing Pochettino’s coaching staff are included.

Pochettino signed a two-and-a-half-year contract on 13 November, replacing Carrick after a difficult start to the Premier League season. The club’s Stock Market filing states that the appointment fee will be recognised in its financial accounts for the current quarter. United also confirmed borrowing a further £10m on 16 November, taking the amount drawn on their revolving credit facility to £240m.

Pochettino is United’s ninth full-time managerial appointment since Ferguson’s departure, including Ralf Rangnick’s interim spell. The club have also changed managers during each of the past three seasons.

United’s financial disclosures show that their long-term debt stood at £577.4m on 30 September, while outstanding transfer-fee commitments totalled £417m. Those figures are separate from the cost of appointing and dismissing managers.

A Reuters analysis has put the wider cost of managerial and senior football staff changes above £100m, using a broader calculation. Pochettino now faces the task of improving United’s results, beginning with Sunday’s Premier League trip to Liverpool.

#2085. OLIVER HOLT: Why England CAN now end 62 years of hurt - Thomas Tuchel is intoxicating and I'd tip Jude Bellingham to beat Kylian Mbappe to the next Ballon d'Or... plus my top 10 Three Lions performances

Published: 12:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 13:04 EST, 16 November 2026

The glum face of Lamine Yamal, head in hands, stared out from the front page of the Spanish sports paper AS as it sat on newspaper stands in Madrid on Monday morning. ‘Fin a la racha,’ the headline said. The end of the run.

For Spain football fans, England’s 3-2 dramatic victory over the world champions in the Spanish capital on Sunday evening made this akin to a day of mourning, the first time their team had tasted defeat in 44 matches, an end to a gilded period of invincibility.

For England, the feeling was very different. Because Sunday night in the cauldron of the Metropolitano felt very much like a beginning. Thomas Tuchel has been the head coach for almost two years but this was the moment of his true arrival.

This was the victory that freed us from looking back to the Groundhog Day pain of that World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in Atlanta last summer and allowed us to look forward to a future that seems luminous and full of hope.

This was the victory that allowed us to stop blaming Tuchel for what happened four months ago and start looking forwards again, dreaming about the glories that he might yet deliver. This was the victory that validated Tuchel and why the FA hired him in the first place. This was the victory that allowed us to believe he might be the Messiah after all.

This felt like the moment when he embraced us, with all our quirks and football idiosyncrasies, and we embraced him. He had promised ‘proof of concept’ on the eve of the game and he delivered it with bells on. Tuchel has harnessed the best of the English game and welded it to his principles and the result is intoxicating.

Thomas Tuchel has harnessed the best of the English game to down world champions Spain

Once you have seen England play the way they did for an hour against Spain, you are lost. You are lost to the belief that the 62 years of hurt might really be coming to an end at Wembley in the final of the European Championship in the summer of 2028. You are lost to the idea that, finally, everything is falling into place.

For the 63 minutes up until the sending off of Elliot Anderson, I have never seen an England performance as good as the one that unfolded in the Metropolitano. Spain are the best team in the world and England outclassed them and stupefied them. They were better than them with the ball and better than them without the ball. They were magnificent.

Because of the context, because of the wonder of the stage, because of the odds they faced, England’s victory over Mexico in the grandeur and the mayhem of the mighty Azteca Stadium during the World Cup might edge Sunday’s performance but for pure football, what England delivered in Madrid demands comparison with the best they have played for many a year.

This year’s World Cup came just too soon but now Tuchel and England understand each other perfectly. And now England are purring. They have a manager who commands the players’ respect and they have a group of players that commands the respect of the manager.

Yes, it was just a Nations League group game but it was against one of the best national sides the world has ever seen. England worked so ferociously and attacked so fluently and defended so devotedly that they reached a level that drew admiration even from their opponents.

Many, many things will live long in the memory. James Trafford’s miraculous double save in the dying minutes gets better every time I watch it. Ben White’s goal channels the beauty of Carlos Alberto’s strike for Brazil against Italy in the 1970 World Cup Final, too. Let’s hope that strike, and his superb defensive performance, bring an end to the boos that have been his companion of late.

Jude Bellingham was relentless, tireless and glided through the game against Spain

Tuchel had promised ‘proof of concept’ on the eve of the game and he delivered it

And then there was Jude Bellingham. Just when you think you can’t admire him any more than you do, he delivers a performance like the one he produced against Spain, a performance that lifted him above even the exalted company of the other players on two fine teams.

Bellingham was tireless. He was relentless. He glided past challenges. He thundered into tackles. He dominated midfield. He has the heart and the sheer brilliant indomitability that Bryan Robson possessed.

Bellingham has it in him to be England’s greatest ever player. He needs trophies to fulfil that destiny but maybe, finally, trophies are in reach again.

He has the team around him to do it, which Robson never quite had. Jordan Pickford is a good goalkeeper but Trafford might just be better. Ezri Konsa had his best game for England in Spain. White and Lewis Hall were superb at full back. Little more needs to be said about England’s front six. They are as good as any unit in world football.

Harry Kane, of course, was the best player in the world last year. Some seem to assume that the Ballon d’Or will inevitably pass to Yamal or Kylian Mbappe next. I think it is more likely to be Bellingham.

The man is a colossus. He is a footballer who has everything. He does not know how to be beaten.

Bellingham saw off Barcelona rival Lamine Yamal - and could beat him to the Ballon d'Or

With them together, the sky is the limit. And Bellingham has also proved to be a player of immense mental strength. It was not so long ago that people worried about his discipline but the fortitude he showed when he was being targeted by Argentina at the World Cup was the best answer to that.

He and Kane are England’s axis of ambition on the pitch. Tuchel is lucky to have them and they are lucky to have him, too. The coach has reached the point where his tactics and his team-building are bearing fruit.

Now England have a team-manager package that genuinely need fear nobody. The victory against Spain was a rehearsal for the bigger stage of major tournaments. Going down to 10 men after 63 minutes against the best team in the world might not have been in the script but that is what rehearsals are for.

After Sunday night in the Metropolitano, England are ready for their close-up.

#2084. He played for Bolton Wanderers and Aston Villa - Then won Celebrity Big Brother

Former Premier League star and Serbian international Sasa Curcic earned both fame in his home country and a substantial payout after becoming a reality TV star following his retirement from the game.

As professional footballers reach the end of their playing careers, many are left with difficult decisions over what to do with their futures. Even the luckiest of players only make it until their mid-to-late thirties in the professional game, and the question of what to do after playing contracts dry up is a very real one.

For some, coaching or scouting is an option, while for others there is a clear appeal to a post-playing career in the media. By taking these routes, former players can rely on the experience that they picked up over the decades during which they were involved in the game. Others enter into business, being able to invest as a result of their time in the game.

But for some players, what's missing is the roar of the crowd, and in the case of the former Aston Villa, Bolton Wanderers and Crystal Palace star Sasa Curcic, the former player found a whole new audience as a reality TV star once his playing days were over.

Sasa Curcic arrived in England having already impressed in his home city of Belgrade. Having first signed for OFK Beograd in 1991, he moved to Partizan Belgrade two years later, having already made his debut for the FR Yugoslavia — now Serbia & Montenegro — national team at the very start of his professional career.

In the summer of 1995, Bolton Wanderers had just been promoted to the Premier League and were looking to strengthen. Curcic was an obvious talent, so was signed by Bolton’s managerial team of Colin Todd and Roy McFarland as they sought to avoid a quick return to the second-tier.

What are your memories of Sasa Curcic? Let us know in the comments below!

Described by When Saturday Comes as "the greatest thriller at Burnden Park since the iconic Frank Worthington", Curcic was given a free role in the Bolton midfield, but he was unable to keep his team in the Premier League; they were relegated back in bottom place in the table.

But having tasted life in the Premier League with Bolton, Curcic wanted to stay there following the club's relegation, and at the start of the 1996-97 season he left for Aston Villa. It was a disastrous move. Curcic fell out with manager Brian Little, and he left the club in March 1998 for Crystal Palace with just 29 League appearances under his belt. The move from Bolton to Villa was later ranked by The Times as the 12th-worst in the first ten years of the Premier League.

But life at Selhurst Park proved to be no easier for him. He managed just 23 League appearances for Palace before leaving the club in 1999, with his spell in South London best-remembered for his protests against NATO bombing of Serbia while he was playing for Palace. After spells in Major League Soccer and in Scotland with Motherwell, he confirmed his retirement as a player in 2001.

FLW ranks the eight most famous footballers to have played in the Championship at some point in their career.

Having picked up a total of 14 appearances for his national team, Curcic was still well-known in Serbia, and he capitalised on that when he entered the Celebrity Big Brother house for their version of the show in May 2007.

As one of thirteen contestants, Curcic proved that he was still able to get people on his side, and it was confirmed a month later that he'd won the competition, scooping a prize of €50,000 and earning himself some lucrative television commercial work as a result of it.

But fame wouldn't last for him. He left the set of another reality show called Farma — "The Farm" — after just a couple of weeks the following year and faded from view again, eventually resurfacing back in South London in 2015, forming an academy with connections to Crystal Palace. He also had a spell managing, back in his home country. Appointed into the head coach's position at the Belgrade-based club Borac Lazarevac in November 2021, he lasted six months in the position before leaving.

Always a bit of a wild child — Brian Little would later tell a few stories of the midfielder's eccentricities, including "hiring a double-decker booze bus with models for his Aston Villa teammates" — Curcic himself later admitted that moving to England in the first place had been a bit of a mistake: "My dream was to play for Partizan, my team. I should have stayed. I would have my own stand, I’d be manager."

It speaks volumes for the self-confidence that got him to the top of the game in England and his subsequent fall from grace that he continued to believe in the certainty that his career would have ended up so differently had he stayed in Serbia in the first place. And Bolton Wanderers fans of a certain age certainly still remember the role he played following their original return to the Premier League.

#2082. Bruno Fernandes breaks silence on Man Utd contract offer

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Bruno Fernandes has been Manchester United’s most creative player since his arrival to the club in 2020.

The 32-year-old is approaching the final months of his current deal, which expires at the end of the season. United do have the option to extend his contract by another 12 months, keeping him at Old Trafford until 2028.

While they can extend his contract for a year, Manchester United are actively pursuing a deal to tie Bruno Fernandes beyond 2028.

Bruno Fernandes himself has now confirmed that the club have offered him a new contract, but the midfielder has made it clear that he does not want discussions about his future to become a priority right now.

Fernandes confirmed that an offer had been made but dismissed suggestions that he was holding out for a better salary or a longer agreement.

“The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay,” he told Sky Sports.

He also insisted that money has never been the reason behind his decision to remain at United, despite having opportunities to move elsewhere in previous transfer windows.

“If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here,” Fernandes said.

The Portugal international added that he could have earned considerably more by accepting offers from other clubs, but always chose to continue his career in Manchester.

Fernandes revealed that discussions initially took place towards the end of last season and continued when the players returned for pre-season.

However, the United captain believes the current situation at the club makes it the wrong time to focus on his personal future.

“We came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side,” he explained.

“I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.”

Fernandes has been one of United’s most influential players since arriving from Sporting in 2020. He has scored 75 Premier League goals for the club and set a new competition record for assists in a single season last term.

Bruno’s comments don’t sound like he is holding United hostage demanding more pay or refusing to sign a new one. The intention as told by Bruno Fernandes just show his leadership trait about putting the team first. He has no immediate intention of making his contract situation the centre of attention. That will be a sign of encouragement for the fans as well.

Manchester United need to start winning games again. When they do and surely Bruno Fernandes will be at the centre of it, the contract talks can resume and take priority.

#2081. He played for Plymouth Argyle & Bristol Rovers - his career then ended in jail

The former Plymouth, Bristol Rovers and Wycombe Wanderers forward is in trouble with the law, and this is far from the first time that this has happened.

The former EFL forward Chris Zebroski is back in trouble with the law again. Appearing at Swindon Magistrates' Court on the 7th October, Zebroski pleaded guilty to assault causing actual bodily harm following an incident which was described as an "alcohol-fuelled attack" in which "the 39-year-old headbutted the older man and knocked out one of his teeth, leaving him with a significant purple bruise under his eye."

Zebroski had been appointed as a player-coach at Southern League side Gosport Borough during the summer.

Chris Zebroski started his career at Swindon Town, but moved to Plymouth Argyle after failing to be offered a senior contract at The County Ground, following a spell with non-league Cirencester City. But he first hit the headlines for all the wrong reasons in August 2007 after he was sacked by the club for gross misconduct following an altercation in the bar during their pre-season tour of Austria the previous month, which left the club captain Paul Wotton with cuts to his head.

Zebroski moved on to Millwall and then to Wycombe Wanderers, but his legal issues continued to pile up. After going on loan to Torquay United, where he was a success in his first season with 19 goals for them in the National League throughout the 2007-08 season, he was given a 12-month community order and a fine for kicking and punching a soldier in a street fight in Torquay in August 2010.

What are your memories of Chris Zebroski as a player? Let us know in the comments below!

He left Wycombe in 2011 to return to Torquay before moving on to Bristol Rovers, After one unsuccessful season there, he joined Cheltenham Town, but midway through his first season at Whaddon Road he had his contract cancelled after repeatedly pulling out of the first-team squad at short notice.

His next move was into the non-league game with Eastleigh, but at the end of the 2012-13 season he was picked up by Newport County. Again, he was a success on the pitch, with 12 goals in 35 League Two appearances as the Exiles finished 14th in League Two, but again his extracurricular activities would come to catch up with him.

The law would come to catch up with Zebroski again in the summer of 2015, and this time the matter at hand was far more serious. His second season at Rodney Parade had been less successful than his first, with seven goals scored in 36 appearances, but he found himself back in court in July 2015, pleading guilty to four charges of robbery, attempted robbery and assault in relation to two incidents.

The first of these incidents had come in December 2014, when Zebroski crashed his BMW into a taxi and then attacked a witness - another taxi driver - who filmed him when he got out of the car, trying to take his mobile phone from him.

The BBC reported at the time that: "Zebroski hit Mr Madhu [one of the taxi drivers] in the side of the head and tried to wrestle his mobile phone from him before taking and smashing it. Mr Vladimirej [the other taxi driver] ran off so Zebroski chased him, pushed him to the ground and punched him at least 10 times, saying "give me your phone."" He was also found to have assaulted and attempted to rob two men the following February.

In mitigation, Zebroski's counsel pleaded that his client had an alcohol problem, but neither the court nor his employers were impressed by this explanation. He was sentenced to four years and four months in prison, and had his contract terminated by Newport County.

He was released after serving two years of his prison sentence, and later claimed that he had come close to re-signing for Newport County after leaving prison. At the time, Zebroski said that, "To get sent to jail had a big impact, a massive wake-up call," and that, "Playing in jail, it definitely built my character."

This time there were no further offers from EFL clubs, and Zebroski instead ended up as a non-league journeyman, playing for numerous clubs before arriving at Gosport in the summer as a player/coach, and on the pitch, this hasn't been a bad season for Gosport, who are mid-table in the Southern League Premier Division South.

But it's been a different matter behind the scenes. Manager Simon Lane was sacked just two games into the season, but his replacement, Jermaine McGlashan, left the club for personal reasons on the 7th October, meaning that they're already onto their third manager of the season. Whether it's a coincidence or not that McGlashan left Gosport on the same day that Zebroski pleaded guilty to the latest set of charges brought against him is unknown.

What is clear about Chris Zebroski's story is that he has been given plenty of chances. After the incidents at Plymouth, Torquay, Cheltenham and Newport, he managed to find someone who would take him on again, but whether this will be the case should he be sentenced to time in prison again is unknown. Zebroski passed forty years of age at the end of October 2026, and his contract position with Gosport will remain unclear until the cost of his latest loss of control is confirmed.

Fans of the clubs for whom he played may well be left wondering what he could have been capable of had he been able to stay on the right side of the law throughout his playing career. And any chances of launching a successful coaching career may already have been blighted by his latest legal problems.

Given that there have been almost two decades since getting sacked by Plymouth and his current predicament during which he might have successfully tackled the underlying issues which lead to these outbreaks of violence, it doesn't seem especially likely that he'll be given many more opportunities within the game.

#2079. Liverpool v Manchester United: Five classic wins at Anfield

Gary Gowers is a sports journalist and the editor of Read Everton, where he leads daily coverage of Everton news, transfers and analysis. He also writes about Manchester City for Read Man City and motorsport for Read Motorsport. A former accountant, he became a freelance writer in 2011 and has written for BBC Sport and Metro.

From Diego Forlan’s unforgettable double to Juan Mata’s spectacular volley, Manchester United have enjoyed some memorable victories at Anfield over the years.

With Mauricio Pochettino preparing for his first match in charge against Liverpool on Sunday, we look back at five occasions when United emerged victorious from one of English football’s fiercest fixtures.

United travelled to Anfield on 19 April 1997 knowing Liverpool could overtake them at the top of the Premier League with a victory. Instead, centre-back Gary Pallister scored twice with headers from David Beckham deliveries, either side of John Barnes’s equaliser.

Andy Cole added a third after the interval, heading home from Gary Neville’s cross following an error by Liverpool goalkeeper David James. The victory helped Sir Alex Ferguson’s side take a decisive step towards retaining the Premier League title, which they secured the following month.

Fresh from winning the Treble, United returned to Anfield for a remarkable match in September 1999. Jamie Carragher headed into his own net inside three minutes before Andy Cole doubled United’s advantage.

Sami Hyypia pulled a goal back for Liverpool, but Carragher’s second own goal restored the visitors’ two-goal lead. Patrik Berger reduced the deficit again, and United faced a difficult finish after Cole was sent off for a second bookable offence. Despite playing the closing stages with 10 men, Ferguson’s side held on for a 3-2 victory.

Diego Forlan had endured a frustrating start to his United career before producing a performance that supporters would remember for years. The Uruguayan opened the scoring after Liverpool goalkeeper Jerzy Dudek failed to gather the ball, allowing him to finish from close range.

Forlan added a second just minutes later, beating Dudek at his near post to put United in control. Sami Hyypia pulled one back for Liverpool, but Ferguson’s side held on for a victory that proved valuable in their successful pursuit of the 2002-03 Premier League title. Forlan’s double also inspired a terrace song that remains familiar to United supporters.

Few United victories at Anfield have been as dramatic as the one secured by John O’Shea in March 2007. Liverpool had enjoyed the better opportunities, and United’s task became harder when Paul Scholes was sent off late in the second half.

With a goalless draw appearing increasingly likely, Cristiano Ronaldo’s free-kick was parried by goalkeeper Pepe Reina. Substitute O’Shea reacted quickest, firing the rebound high into the net in stoppage time. The unexpected winner gave United three valuable points on their way to reclaiming the Premier League title.

Juan Mata produced one of the most memorable individual performances in this fixture during Louis van Gaal’s first season as United manager. The Spaniard opened the scoring after 14 minutes, finishing a move involving Ander Herrera, before doubling United’s lead with a spectacular scissor-kick volley after half-time.

Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard had been sent off just 38 seconds after coming on as a substitute at the interval. Daniel Sturridge reduced the deficit, while Wayne Rooney missed a late penalty, but United held on for a 2-1 victory. Mata’s second goal remains one of the outstanding moments of United’s Premier League visits to Anfield.

Those five victories underline the different ways United have succeeded at Anfield, from outstanding individual performances to late winners and determined defensive displays. Pochettino now has an opportunity to begin his managerial reign with a memorable result against United’s biggest rivals.

Which United victory at Anfield is your favourite? Were you there for Forlan’s double, O’Shea’s winner or Mata’s volley? Share your memories in the comments below.

#2078. Chelsea Monitor Jarrod Bowen And Crysencio Summerville

Chelsea’s wide-player search has moved back into focus after the Guardian reported that the club are monitoring West Ham pair Jarrod Bowen and Crysencio Summerville.

The update lands during a busy early market for Xabi Alonso’s incoming rebuild.

The Guardian’s latest transfer round-up states that Chelsea like both West Ham forwards, while an earlier report noted Chelsea and Manchester United had tracked Summerville.

That same earlier update also said Aston Villa, Chelsea and Everton had expressed interest in Bowen.

West Ham pulling away at Stamford Bridge 👀Jarrod Bowen stuns Chelsea early before Crysencio Summerville doubles the lead. pic.twitter.com/Ktwr4pKZGH

Alonso officially begins work on July 1, with Chelsea confirming he has signed a four-year contract to lead the men’s team.

The winger search is not just about adding more attacking names. It is about identifying profiles who can quickly give Chelsea sharper final-third decisions.

Bowen would offer immediate Premier League output, penalty-box timing and a direct threat from the right.

Summerville, meanwhile, fits the younger, explosive one-v-one profile that would sit neatly inside Alonso’s longer-term wing plan.

Read Chelsea has already tracked the separate Summerville angle, but this latest dual link sharpens the picture.

Chelsea appear to be testing two different solutions to the same problem: proven reliability or higher-upside acceleration.

With pre-season closing in, that is exactly the sort of market check Alonso needs before deciding how much of Chelsea’s attacking rebuild should lean on speed, touchline width and more ruthless wide output.

#2077. Thomas Frank announced as Crystal Palace boss as he eyes raid on Chelsea set-piece guru marginalised under Xabi Alonso

By BOBBY MANZI, FOOTBALL REPORTER and KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER

Published: 10:07 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 13:08 EST, 16 November 2026

Thomas Frank has been unveiled as Crystal Palace’s new manager on a two-and-a-half-year deal.

Frank has been out of work since being sacked by Tottenham Hotspur in February and has taken a significant pay cut to take over at Palace, who languish at the bottom of the Premier League.

However, he will earn more than his predecessor, Pierre Sage, who was sacked last week after winning just two of his ten league matches in charge.

New Palace boss Frank said: ‘It's an honour to sit here and be in charge of this fantastic Football Club. I'm really, really looking forward to it.

‘Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League. I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I'm really looking forward to meeting them.’

Across his spells at Brentford and Tottenham, Frank has managed 178 Premier League matches with a 34 per cent win rate.

Palace are set to approach Chelsea about Bernardo Cueva, who worked with Frank at Brentford before being poached to become the Blues' set-piece specialist.

We are pleased to confirm the appointment of Thomas Frank as Manager 🤝ℹ️ https://t.co/2wUzZAGt4S pic.twitter.com/zv2vMPGPFz

Palace are set to approach Chelsea about Cueva (right), who worked with Frank at Brentford

But Cueva may now be elevated back to the forefront of football if Palace can strike an agreement to bring him in to join Frank’s backroom staff. It is said Chelsea paid Brentford around £1million in compensation to hire him in 2024 at a time when his stock was high.

Cueva arrived at Chelsea in 2024. However, Daily Mail Sport revealed in the last summer how the 39-year-old Mexican’s role was changing after two seasons of work as Xabi Alonso’s side hired Austin MacPhee from Aston Villa as their new lead on set-plays.

Cueva has not been seen since then, either in training at Cobham or at matches at Stamford Bridge, but continued to work for Chelsea in more of an analytical role behind the scenes.

Club sources stressed at the time that it should not be seen as a demotion, and he is still listed on the first-team staff section of the website under the title ‘technical analyst’.

Chelsea are due to play Palace in two weeks' time at the Bridge on Wednesday, December 2.

Chelsea previously identified Cueva as a prime candidate for a role which had been vacant since Anthony Barry exited for Bayern Munich. Cueva, who also holds a UEFA Pro Licence through the Football Association, was regarded as an impressive acquisition in 2024.

Before joining Brentford in 2020 and helping them secure promotion to the Premier League, Cueva was at Chivas in his homeland of Mexico. He has also had a role with Norway men's national team.

#2076. Moises Caicedo And Kendry Paez Give Chelsea World Cup Signal

Ecuador’s late World Cup surge has given Chelsea a useful development signal through Moises Caicedo and Kendry Paez before Xabi Alonso’s first pre-season friendly on 28 July.

Chelsea confirmed that Caicedo and Paez reached the Round of 32 after Ecuador’s dramatic 2-1 win over Germany.

For Alonso, the contrast between the two Chelsea midfielders matters as much as the result.

Caicedo captained Ecuador through the pressure game, with We Ain’t Got No History highlighting the Chelsea midfielder’s leadership role in a win that rescued their tournament.

Paez, meanwhile, sits in a different phase of his rise.

That should not worry Chelsea. FIFA identified Paez as one of the tournament’s wonderkids, but Chelsea’s bigger win is that he can absorb elite-tournament preparation without carrying a defining role too soon.

Read Chelsea has already looked at how Alonso must handle Paez’s development curve, and this knockout place sharpens that argument.

Alonso inherits a midfield loaded with senior names, transfer noise and immediate pressure.

Caicedo gives Chelsea the proven pillar. Paez gives them the controlled upside.

Ecuador’s run now gives Chelsea both at once.

For Chelsea, that is the ideal succession picture: leadership today, patience for tomorrow.
